senses.definition: Moving forward with clear, real progress toward a goal.
senses.caution: A positive, slightly formal phrase. Use it when the progress is real and visible, since it sounds hollow if you cannot say what has improved.
senses.example: The team is making strides on the migration: two of the five services are already live.

cues.text: At a status update you tell your director that the team has moved noticeably ahead on the migration this quarter. You want the idiom, built on a word for long steps, that says the progress is real.
A colleague asks how the new hire is doing, and you say she is improving quickly and visibly in her first month. What idiom, built on a word for long steps, do you use?
Your friend has been learning Spanish for six months and can now hold a real conversation. You want the idiom, built on a word for long steps, that praises how far she has come.

distractors: Not saying what you think, so as to avoid an argument.
To decide what to do as you go instead of following a plan.
To explain something clearly so that others can follow it.
To ask someone for advice because they know the subject well.
Fully prepared in advance, with every detail checked.
